newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia open to NASA talks on space station delay.
newsitem.headline: Russia open to NASA talks on space station delay.

text.p: The Russian Space Agency said on Thursday it was happy to discuss its problems with the United States after NASA announced a special mission to Moscow to investigate delays in Russia's share of a new international space station.

NASA chief Dan Goldin told congressmen on Wednesday he was sending a team of experts to Russia in March and would follow himself in April to determine whether NASA needed to launch a contingency plan to get space station Alpha off the ground while waiting for the Russians to complete their components.

"Promises no longer count, it's action," Goldin told a House of Representatives Appropriations panel, two days after Russian Space Agency head Yuri Koptev announced cash shortages would delay the launch of the first Alpha module by seven months.

Anatoly Tkachev, a spokesman for the Russian Space Agency, said NASA officials were quite welcome to visit its sites and discuss the circumstances which caused the delay of the first Alpha module launch to June 1998 from November 1997.
"I am not aware of the statement but a visit from NASA is a quite normal procedure," he told Reuters. "We always pursue a policy of openness with our partners on our circumstances."
A fire on Sunday aboard the ageing Russian orbital station Mir, with an American and German on board, did little to bolster global confidence in Moscow's space programme.
Russian officials, including Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, have assured Washington that there will be enough money to complete their part of the $37-billion Alpha project.
Tkachev noted that Chernomyrdin discussed space cooperation with U.S. Vice-President Al Gore during their twice-yearly meeting in the United States earlier this month.
Alpha, also funded by the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan, is due to be complete by 2003.
Russia is building the first module, a cargo section, and the third, a service area where cosmonauts will live and work.

A delay in launching the first module will also delay launch of the second stage, a docking module being built in the United States. After the third module, other parts of the station will be attached in stages up to 2003.

Goldin expressed doubts to the House panel that Russia would be able to deliver its modules on time, but said the National Aeronautics and Space Administration hoped to keep the "end date" of the project in place.

Some U.S. congressmen accuse Moscow of not pulling its weight. James Sensenbrenner, chairman of the House Science Committee and a fierce critic of Russia's involvement, said last week the service module delay could "unravel the whole project".

NASA's contingency plans include the construction of an Interim Control Module, which would keep the embryonic station in proper orbit while waiting for the launch of the Russian service module, Goldin said.

Koptev complained on Monday that Moscow's state financing of the space sector was just one seventh of that in Soviet days, but added that cooperation with foreign firms was now offering domestic companies a lifeline worth millions of dollars.
